title: Cop31 live: ‘Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs’ - UN chief hits out at industry lobbying
text:
'The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.' - UN chief
Oliver Milman
Guterres launches into a plea for accelerated action to cut emissions and takes direct aim at the fossil fuel industry. The UN chief has already called on countries to push forward a phase out of fossil fuels, rather than merely hinting at it, here at Cop.
“The case for fossil fuels is collapsing,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs. And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”
“It’s time to kick the habit – and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said. Guterres likes a good pun and one of his final climate speeches has a decent one: “It’s make or bake time.”
Nazar Mohammed Saeed Amedi, president of Iraq, is citing the country’s past as Mesopotamia, “the cradle of human civilisation” and one of the first birthplaces of agriculture, and contrasting it with the challenges that climate change is already bringing it. He says the loss of arable land and projected hit to water security will jeapordise its food security. He’s calling for more support for a green economy.
We’re now hearing from Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov, leader of Turkmenistan. He’s speaking about efforts to modernise his country’s energy infrastructure and calling for greater climate resilience in the face of worsening weather.
Turkmenistan is an oil and gas producer that has become infamous for its vast emissions of methane, a potent planet-heating gas that is wastefully vented from fossil fuel infrastructure. In August, my colleague Damian Carrington, who has uncovered some of the country’s worst excesses, reported on early successful efforts to plug some of these “mind-boggling” leaks.
The first national leader to speak is Mohamed Cheikh El Ghazouani, President of Mauritania, who is calling for an increase in the assistance given to countries most affected by climate change. “Despite the limited carbon footprint it has, Mauritiania has been suffering greatly from climate change and its consequences, including drought, land degradation and coastal erosion.” He says these have hit the economic fabric of the country, particularly in rural areas.
Murat Kurum, Turkey’s climate minister and Cop31 president, is now up. He’s detailing the weather extremes battering countries around the world, while making the case for how climate action is in countries’ national interests – by boosting energy security, for instance. He’s making some similar points to Bowen on the many obstacles to global cooperation.
“Our collective success depends on our ability to identify common interests,” he says.
When it comes to food, water and climate risks – which recognise no borders – there can only be common ground, he says.
“Let us make Antalya a symbol city for action,” he says.
Unsurprisingly, neither of the co-hosts mentioned their own countries’ expansions of fossil fuel infrastructure that have undermined their credibility somewhat – Australia as a major exporter of coal, oil and gas, and Turkey having just celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields this week.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and president of the negotiations, is framing the talks as a challenge for multilaterism in the face of threats from worsening weather to geopolitics.
“It’s no exaggeration to say the world is facing a polycrisis – not challenges on one front, but on multiple fronts, all at once.”
His answer is a resounding yes, for global cooperation. “While the challenge is growing, so is our agency. Before Paris the world was heading to nearly 4c of warming. Now it’s closer to 2.6C.”
He’s underscoring the existential nature of climate crisis for Pacific islands – particularly from overshooting the 1.5C target – as well as the small share of climate finance they receive.
He concludes: “Together, we can demonstrate that multilateral cooperation still matters, and can deliver in the critical moment.”
Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), is sweeping through the scientific findings that underpin everything that is being discussed in Antalya. CO2 in the atmosphere is 50% higher than in the preindustrial era. Land and oceans cannot keep up. The Earth energy imbalance is at its highest level since measurements began in 1960. The planet is accumulating heat at an increasing rate. The past 12 years are the warmest on record.
But along with the gloom are some reasons for hope. Saulo is celebrating the work of the WMO in observing the planet – able to predict disasters before they strike – and the rollout of early warning systems. These are “giving countries time to prepare and protect”, she says, while calling for greater investments in them.
The President of the UN general assembly, Khalilur Rahman, has just opened the segment for heads of state and government. He’s making a plea for action and multilaterism before leaders of dozens of nations make their contributions – with a reminder about what really matters. “Speeches do not cool our planet. Decisions and deliveries do.”
The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey.
Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict.
“National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya.
“We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face. Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said.
In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”
This week I’ve been speaking to young climate activists at Cop31. Today I spoke to Sohanur Rahman, 29, from Bangladesh, who survived a super-cyclone as a child.
He became a key figure in the fight against climate change in Bangladesh after founding YouthNet for Climate Justice in 2016.
“I feel a deep sense of urgency, frustration and cautious hope as we approach Cop31. After attending five Cops, I am no longer satisfied with promises. I want to see whether those promises are actually changing people’s lives.
“For countries like Bangladesh, climate change is not a distant threat. It is already affecting us through extreme heat, cyclones, floods, river erosion and salinity. Behind every negotiation are people who cannot afford another decade of delay. I am particularly concerned that climate-vulnerable countries are still expected to borrow money to deal with the consequences of a crisis they contributed very little to. Climate finance must be accessible, predictable and primarily grant-based.
“Despite my frustration, I remain hopeful. I see hope in young people organising in their communities, women leading local adaptation efforts, Indigenous peoples protecting nature and frontline communities developing solutions despite limited resources. They remind me that a different future is possible: one where people can live safely, work with dignity and thrive without destroying the natural systems on which we all depend.
“My hope is that CopP31 in Antalya becomes a turning point from promises to implementation. We need climate finance that reaches frontline communities, responsible businesses, a just transition for workers, stronger international cooperation and institutions that deliver on their commitments.”
UK heatwaves could cost London more than £25bn in lost productivity over the next decade, the mayor of London will tell world leaders.
Through analysis from City Hall, which also estimates the 2026 heatwaves cost the capital about £2.5bn in lost productivity, Sadiq Khan will underline the economic consequences of extreme heat, as high temperatures make it harder for people to work effectively.
“The climate sceptics argue that these investments are unaffordable,” Khan will tell Cop. “But the only thing we cannot afford is to do nothing.
“Even if you can see past the devastating implications for human health, the long-term economic impact of extreme heat alone will be astronomical,” the mayor is expected to say. “If the scenes we saw this summer became the standard, it could cost London’s economy more than £25 billion over the next ten years.”
Khan will also warn that record breaking heat in the UK is already taking a devastating toll on people’s health, businesses and public services, with thousands of vulnerable people losing their lives to heat-related causes.
“Climate disaster is no longer the stuff of some distant dystopia,” Khan will say. “It’s killing people, harming communities and impacting our economies right now. And failing to protect ourselves from the perils we face – or prepare ourselves for worse to come – would be a dereliction of duty.”
Erdogan spends some time thanking people and explaining how the rooms at the venue are named after legendary Turkish figures before launching into an almost Deep Ecology-style lament.
“As humanity we only have one roof over our home, namely the sky, as humanity we only have one garden, namely the Earth,” he said. “Let me state this plainly – we have no other sky, no other Earth, no other seas, oceans or forests.”
Greed for excessive consumption is causing the “deepest existential crisis” in human history, he said. “We all know well a forest in flames, a river running dry, a polluted sea all inflict pain on the entire planet,” he said. “No country is exempt from this pain.”
Progress has been made at these annual UN climate talks but there’s been a lack of implementation, Erdogan says in front of a screen that blares ‘Implementation Cop.’ He added “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow.”
